clue.text: Unfortunately Jay came in late, missing the end of feature film

indicators.note: the word losing its end drops its final letter before anything else happens
something that happens unfortunately goes wrong, so the letters fall into a muddled new order

parts.note: taken as written
late with its last letter dropped

explanation.surface: Someone called Jay turned up late and missed the end of the feature film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feature film' looks like part of the cinema story but it is the definition: Calamity Jane is the 1953 Doris Day musical.
explanation.definitionFit: Calamity Jane is the title of a full-length Hollywood musical starring Doris Day.

clue.text: Worry about place to put scrap firearm

indicators.note: about means going around, so one word wraps the other

parts.note: to worry is to care
a bin is where you throw scraps away

explanation.surface: Someone frets over where to dump an old gun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrap' looks like a verb meaning discard, which makes the surface about getting rid of the firearm.
explanation.definitionFit: A carbine is a short rifle, a type of shoulder-fired gun.

clue.text: State chains wildcat

indicators.note: to state something is to say it out loud, so the word is judged by its sound

parts.note: chains are made of links, and links is pronounced the same as the cat

explanation.surface: A government shackles a wild animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' looks like a nation or region, but it is the instruction to say a word out loud.
explanation.definitionFit: The lynx is a wild member of the cat family with tufted ears.

clue.text: The Scottish play hard after BTEC and MA churned out

indicators.note: after sends the hard abbreviation to the end, behind the reworked qualifications
churning stirs things up, so these letters come out in a new order

parts.note: the two qualifications taken letter for letter
H is the pencil abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A grumble that a hard play follows on the heels of mass-produced qualifications.
explanation.walkthrough: A BTEC is a British vocational qualification and an MA a master's degree. 'After' places the hard letter at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Actors superstitiously avoid naming Shakespeare's Macbeth in a theatre, calling it the Scottish play instead.

clue.text: Small computers Eliot put on board

parts.note: board can mean a table, as in bed and board
the poet T. S. Eliot gives his initials

explanation.surface: Eliot set some little computers down on the board.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, one piece 'put on' another sits after it; T. S. Eliot is the poet of The Waste Land.
explanation.definitionFit: Tablets are flat, handheld touchscreen computing devices like the iPad.

clue.text: Charlie preserved meat

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a charlie is a fool
second meaning: meat cured and dried in strips

explanation.surface: Charlie has cured some meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charlie' is British slang for an idiot, not a person's name here.
explanation.definitionFit: One word means both a contemptible idiot and beef cured by drying, as in jerked beef.

clue.text: Easy way to identify 30's younger brother in the sauna?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a casual phrase saying something is no trouble

definitions.text: way to identify 30's younger brother in the sauna?
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the man who once claimed he was unable to perspire would be the dry one

explanation.surface: A jokey tip for spotting a royal among sweating sauna users.
explanation.walkthrough: 30-across is Princess Anne; her younger brother Prince Andrew claimed in a 2019 interview that he could not sweat.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'no sweat' means a task is no trouble at all, a colloquial synonym for easy.

clue.text: Lad from granite city who's quite beefy?

definitions.text: Lad from granite city who's quite beefy?

parts.note: surface reading: a burly young man from Scotland's granite city
setter's reading: the boy's name plus the city name make a breed of beef cattle

explanation.surface: A well-built young man from Aberdeen.
explanation.walkthrough: Aberdeen is nicknamed the Granite City and Angus is a Scottish boy's name, so the beefy lad is the cattle breed.
explanation.definitionFit: Aberdeen Angus is a famous Scottish breed of black beef cattle, so it is literally beefy.

clue.text: Novel, chapter1 p5: "Beast of Whitechapel"

indicators.note: novel means new and different, so the letters are made into a fresh arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
the Roman numeral for one
taken as written
the answer to 5 Down

explanation.surface: A citation from a novel, chapter one, page five, describing a notorious monster of Whitechapel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like the book being cited, but it is the anagram signal; '5' stands for the answer to 5 Down.
explanation.definitionFit: The unidentified Victorian serial killer operated in London's Whitechapel district in 1888.

clue.text: Darkly handsome, Corbyn strangely overwhelms one

indicators.note: to overwhelm is to engulf, so one piece swallows the other
doing something strangely means doing it oddly, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the politician's name taken as written
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An odd claim that a handsome Jeremy Corbyn bowls everyone over.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeremy Corbyn is a former leader of Britain's Labour Party.
explanation.definitionFit: Byronic describes a brooding, moody attractiveness like that of the poet Lord Byron.

clue.text: Retired Arab drinking first coffee made by this person?

indicators.note: drinking takes something inside, so one piece holds the other
retired means gone back, so the word is read in the backward direction

parts.note: taken as written
1st, the ordinal abbreviation, with the figure read as I

explanation.surface: A retired Arab man takes his first coffee of the day.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition shares its words with the wordplay picture: the coffee is made by the one named.
explanation.definitionFit: A barista is a worker in a coffee bar who prepares espresso drinks.

clue.text: Wet weather right by road from Newcastle to Alnwick?

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for right
the A1 runs from Newcastle up to Alnwick, so it is the A1 going north, N

explanation.surface: A soggy forecast for the drive up the road from Newcastle to Alnwick.
explanation.walkthrough: Alnwick is a Northumberland town north of Newcastle on the A1, Britain's main east-coast trunk road; the 1 is read as I.
explanation.definitionFit: Rain is falling water from clouds, the commonest kind of wet weather.

clue.text: Handle First Lady held in both hands

indicators.note: something held in is gripped inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: L and R, left and right
Eve was the first woman in Genesis

explanation.surface: A president's wife grips a handle with both hands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First Lady' suggests a president's wife, but it is the first woman in the Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: A lever is a bar or handle you pull or push to operate a machine.

clue.text: Bill for the magistrate

definitions.meaning: second meaning: old British slang for a judge or magistrate

explanation.surface: An invoice sent to the magistrate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' reads as an invoice, but it is a bird's mouthpart.
explanation.definitionFit: A beak is a bird's horny mouth, and in British slang a magistrate sitting in court.

clue.text: Desert animal arrived then left

parts.note: arrived means came
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: An animal in the desert came and went.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' reads as departed, but here it is the side.
explanation.definitionFit: The camel is the classic beast of burden of the Sahara and Arabian deserts.

clue.text: Doctor unwell? That's a bit boring

parts.note: DR is the abbreviation for doctor
unwell means ill

explanation.surface: Complaining that a sick doctor is rather tedious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bit boring' sounds like mildly dull, but it means a tool bit that bores holes.
explanation.definitionFit: A drill is a tool whose bit bores holes, so it is a boring implement.

clue.text: English trees? Nonsense!

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English
two trees, the yew and the ash

explanation.surface: Someone scoffs at the idea of trees being English.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyewash is informal for talk meant to deceive, i.e. rubbish or humbug.

clue.text: Nick caught rodent in school

indicators.note: in places one group of letters inside another

parts.note: SCH is the abbreviation for school
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
a rat is a rodent

explanation.surface: A boy called Nick catches a rat at school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' looks like a name, but it is a small cut.
explanation.definitionFit: A nick and a scratch are both small superficial marks or cuts on a surface.

clue.text: Beginning new climb

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for new
a climb is an ascent

explanation.surface: Starting out on a fresh climb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beginning' reads as a noun but stands for an adjective: just coming into being.
explanation.definitionFit: Nascent describes something just starting to exist or develop, i.e. in its beginning stages.

clue.text: Sulphur smell here exposed parasite

parts.note: S is the chemical symbol for sulphur
pong is British slang for a bad smell

indicators.note: exposed means uncovered, so the word loses its outside letters and only its middle is kept

parts.note: the inside letters of here

explanation.surface: A sulphurous stink reveals a parasite hidden here.
explanation.definitionFit: A sponger lives off other people's generosity, a human parasite.

clue.text: Catch 4 Down reportedly in swingers' bar

parts.note: to catch is to trap

indicators.note: reportedly means as heard said, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: 4 Down is tablets, and E is slang for an ecstasy tablet, so the plural is said like the letters ees

explanation.surface: Catching drug pills going round in a bar where partner-swappers gather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swingers' bar' suggests a nightspot for swapping partners; the swingers are acrobats.
explanation.definitionFit: A trapeze is a horizontal bar hung on ropes on which circus acrobats swing.

clue.text: Former PM, force in development of Labour

indicators.note: in places one letter inside the other group
development reshapes something, so these letters are built into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
F is the physics symbol for force

explanation.surface: A former prime minister was a force in shaping the Labour Party.
explanation.walkthrough: Arthur Balfour was Conservative prime minister 1902-05, so the Labour link is a false trail.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Balfour served as British prime minister from 1902 to 1905.

clue.text: British/Germanic settlers joined girl band

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for British
the Angles were a Germanic people who settled in England

explanation.surface: British and Germanic settlers joined an all-female group.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bangles were an American all-female pop group famous for Walk Like an Egyptian.

clue.text: Expose Vogue scandal

parts.note: to out someone is to expose them
something in vogue is all the rage

explanation.surface: Revealing a scandal at Vogue magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vogue' reads as the fashion magazine, but it means a craze.
explanation.definitionFit: An outrage is a shocking event provoking public indignation, much like a scandal.

clue.text: Recess not approved?

parts.note: no expresses not
approved means okayed, OK

explanation.surface: A query whether a break has been refused.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recess' reads as a holiday or break, but it is a small alcove.
explanation.definitionFit: A nook is a small corner or recess in a room.

clue.text: Female isn't commonly dim

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for female
ain't is the colloquial form of isn't

explanation.surface: A rude remark that a woman is not usually stupid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dim' reads as stupid, but it means indistinct.
explanation.definitionFit: A faint light or outline is a dim one, barely perceptible.

clue.text: Halt loads of money going west

indicators.note: in an across clue west is leftward, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: pots of money means lots of it

explanation.surface: Stopping a fortune from heading westwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To halt is to come to a stop, a direct verb synonym.

clue.text: Wee child leaving island farmer's store

indicators.note: leaving means departing, so that letter is taken out

parts.note: bairn is Scots for a child
I is the abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: A small child leaves an island for a farmer's shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wee' looks like plain 'small', but it hints at the Scots word for a child.
explanation.definitionFit: A barn is a farm building used for storing grain, hay and equipment.

clue.text: A sign of submariner surfacing?

indicators.note: in a down clue surfacing means rising, so the word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: Captain Nemo commands the submarine Nautilus in Jules Verne

explanation.surface: Wondering whether there is a sign of a submarine man coming up.
explanation.definitionFit: An omen is a portent, a sign of something to come.

clue.text: At university, graduate beginning to enjoy higher status

parts.note: being up means at university in British usage
grad is short for graduate

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of enjoy

explanation.surface: A university graduate starts to enjoy a rise in standing.
explanation.walkthrough: In British English a student is 'up' at university, e.g. up at Oxford.
explanation.definitionFit: An upgrade is an improvement to a better class or rank, a rise in status.

clue.text: Pop broadcast lie, fabricated

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered widely, so the letters are strewn into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
fabricated means made

explanation.surface: A pop star's on-air lie turns out to have been made up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop' reads as pop music, but it is a fizzy drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Pop is a fizzy soft drink, and limeade is a lime-flavoured fizzy drink.

clue.text: VIP battered cane spinners

indicators.note: battered means knocked out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A dignitary was struck by people twirling walking sticks.
explanation.definitionFit: Princess Anne, the Princess Royal, is a senior royal and so a very important person.
